text: Discovery told you what's there. This lesson is about the act of actually attaching a classification label to it, and what breaks when that label doesn't travel with the data.

Manual tagging is a person, usually a data owner or steward, applying a label based on judgment. It scales badly on its own, but it catches what automation misses, a spreadsheet that's technically just numbers but is actually a draft of unreleased financial results. Automated tagging uses discovery techniques, pattern matching, metadata scanning, to apply or recommend a label with no human step. It scales to an entire data estate, but it inherits every limitation of the underlying discovery technique. Mature organizations run both, automated as the default fast layer, manual review for the ambiguous or high-stakes cases.

A label only does real work if it's stored as metadata a system can read, a catalog tag, a column property, not a fact that lives in someone's head. And it has to travel with the data. Copy a Confidential table to a spreadsheet, and the label usually doesn't follow, that spreadsheet is now unlabeled Confidential data. Join an Internal table with a Confidential one, and the result should inherit the higher classification, but the join itself doesn't relabel anything automatically. Feed a classified table into a pipeline, and every derived table starts unlabeled unless the classification is explicitly propagated.

The failures in a real classification program happen at these propagation points, not at the initial labeling. And a label that triggers nothing isn't doing its job. A Restricted tag should mean access gets restricted, data gets encrypted, queries get logged, an alert fires on export, automatically. If nothing downstream reads the label, the organization built a filing system, not a security control.
Classification is a property that has to be actively propagated every time data is copied, combined, or transformed. Next up: classification governance, who decides the labels and keeps them current.
